critical: button-name (icon-only buttons with no accessible name): up to 27-30 nodes on the categories list (happy-path run) — the reorder Up/Down arrows (CategoriesTable.tsx) and each row's '...' actions-menu trigger render bare <button> elements with only a lucide icon inside, no aria-label or visible text. A screen-reader user cannot tell these buttons apart at all, on the page whose entire job is reordering and managing rows.

label (form elements without a programmatic label): 3 nodes on the category create form — Name/Slug/Description fields use a bare <label> as a visual sibling of the <input>, with no htmlFor/id pairing and no aria-label. Confirmed directly while writing every spec in this suite: getByLabel() never works against these fields; an XPath sibling lookup off the label's exact text was required everywhere, including for Meta Title/Description, which nest the label inside an extra wrapper div alongside their character counter — a second, distinct instance of the same missing-association pattern.
serious: color-contrast: recurring on every step of the happy-path flow (6-12 nodes per page: login, categories list, and the create form) — likely a small set of shared components/tokens rather than unrelated per-page bugs.
moderate: landmark-unique: flagged on every page in the happy-path flow.
landmark-one-main / page-has-heading-one / region: flagged on the login page specifically.
heading-order: flagged once, on the post-login page.
empty-table-header (minor, folded in here since the schema has no separate minor bucket): 1 node on the categories list — likely the blank actions-column header.
accessibility_summary.coverage_caveat: automated scan only — manual/screen-reader review still needed

concerns: Lighthouse was deliberately left off for every run in this suite to keep CPU usage down on a resource-constrained environment — no performance numbers were collected.

ux_gaps.issue: Reorder Up/Down arrows and the row actions-menu trigger are icon-only with zero accessible name.
Name/Slug/Description/Meta Title/Meta Description labels are not programmatically associated with their inputs anywhere in this form.

A React hydration mismatch (server/client-mismatched inline style, specifically caret-color: transparent) is logged as a console error on the login page's email/password inputs in every run that visits it. Did not block login in any of the 7 runs that hit it. A parallel, structurally similar hydration mismatch was independently found on the storefront app's homepage and products page (see category-storefront-visibility-analysis.json) — two separate Next.js codebases showing the same class of warning raises the odds this is environment/headless-browser noise rather than two coincidentally-identical app bugs, but that is a hypothesis, not a conclusion; still worth a real-browser check.

recommendations.action: Add aria-label to the reorder Up/Down buttons (e.g. 'Move up', 'Move down') and the row actions-menu trigger (e.g. 'Category actions') in CategoriesTable.tsx — critical WCAG button-name violations on the page whose entire purpose is managing these rows.

Associate CategoryForm.tsx's Name/Slug/Description/Meta Title/Meta Description <label> elements with their inputs via htmlFor/id (or wrap the input inside the label) — critical WCAG label violations, and this codebase's own admin CLAUDE.md documents fixing exactly this class of gap elsewhere (e.g. Reviews, Content managers).
Audit the shared color-contrast tokens once rather than treating each page's flagged nodes as separate issues — the same violation recurred on every page in this flow.
Add a <main> landmark and a level-one heading to the login page specifically.
Manually verify the caret-color hydration mismatch in a real browser on both this app's login page and the storefront's homepage/products page before assuming it's test-environment noise.

parent_id (category hierarchy) and icon_name exist on the backend Category model/schema but have no UI anywhere in this admin panel — confirmed gap, not a bug; worth a product decision on whether either is actually needed.
